text:
Short answer: no, don't make anything of it — at least not as your argument.

**Why the panel composition is a weak card**

A four-woman panel is unremarkable in education, where women are a large majority of teachers and a growing majority of school leaders. In most selection processes the panel is composed of role-holders — the board chair, an HR representative, a municipal education director, a staff or parent representative — so the gender mix is usually a by-product of who happens to hold those posts, not a choice. Composition alone tells you nothing about how any individual panel member reasoned.

More practically: if you lead with "the panel was all women," you hand them an easy reply. It reframes you from *a candidate with a documented qualifications question* to *a man who thinks he lost because of women*. Decision-makers, ombudsmen and tribunals all discount that kind of argument fast, and it taints everything else you say. Panel composition is at best weak background context that becomes relevant only *after* you've established that the substantive decision doesn't hold up.

**What is actually strong in your position**

Look at the comparison on its face:

| | You | Appointee |
|---|---|---|
| Teaching licence | Yes | Yes |
| Leadership education | Master's degree | "Courses" |
| Leadership experience | 5 years as deputy principal | None stated |
| Teaching experience | Not stated | 10 years |

On the published description, you appear to hold a formal qualification advantage on the two criteria most specific to the job — leadership education and leadership experience. That's your case. It stands entirely on its own without reference to anyone's gender.

Two caveats worth being honest with yourself about. First, you don't know what was in the announcement versus the full file: she may have substantial unlisted leadership experience, strong references, or a much better interview. Second, principal selections legitimately weigh things that don't appear on paper — vision, staff confidence, fit with a specific school's situation. A panel is usually allowed to prefer a candidate who interviewed better, provided both met the requirements. So "better on paper" is a real argument, not an automatic win.

**The unanswered request is your actual issue right now**

This is the part I'd focus on. In many jurisdictions a public-sector appointment carries a duty to provide written reasons on request, often within a short statutory window — two weeks is a common figure. If that applies where you are, silence is itself a procedural failure and it's the cleanest thing to press.

What I'd do:

1. **Send a written follow-up this week.** Reference your original request by date, restate it, cite the legal basis if you can identify it, and give a deadline. Keep it short and neutral in tone.
2. **Ask for specifics, not a summary.** Request the stated job requirements, the assessment criteria and any scoring, the written comparison of the shortlisted candidates, and the panel's reasoning. Vague reasons are much harder to test.
3. **Only then evaluate.** Once you see how they weighted the criteria, you'll know whether this was a defensible judgement call or a decision that can't be justified against its own stated criteria.
4. **Note deadlines now.** Complaints to an ombudsman, equality body or tribunal usually have time limits running from the decision or from the reasons being given. Find out what yours are before they lapse.

One thing worth knowing: equality legislation in many countries does permit preferring a candidate of an under-represented gender, but typically *only when candidates are otherwise equally qualified*. That cuts in your favour, not against you — if you're better qualified, such a provision wouldn't authorise the appointment. So even on the terrain where gender is legally relevant, your argument is about qualifications.

If it turns out they genuinely can't justify the decision against their own criteria, the pattern of who sat on the panel might become a minor supporting detail. It will never be the argument. Build the case on the paperwork.

If you tell me which country or system this is, I can be more specific about the statutory deadlines and which body handles the complaint.
